utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries, if I understand well. We have to briefly move into closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom, but I already announce that for the remainder of the testimony of this witness, Judge Moloto will be acting Presiding Judge, because I've not attended the beginning of the testimony of that witness. Could we turn into closed session, in order to have the witness enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness RM297. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear me in the language you understand, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge, I always tell the truth, otherwise I say nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm very happy to hear that. Mr. Lukic, according to our records, you're left with 48 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you could hear, we haven't got much left. I'd like to start with a number of questions which have to do with the 11th, the 12th of July, 1995. One of your brothers went to Susnjari with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other brother was handicapped and he went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was evacuated from Potocari to Kladanj, and he is still alive today.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And, luckily enough, he is no longer handicapped. He was never wounded, but he had sciatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please have in e-court P1132. It is the book compiled by Mr. Ruez, which you have been shown previously. We need page 130. 131. It is the school in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were there with Mr. Ruez in this room --

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the closets were there when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you could not recall the basketball equipment being mounted on the walls at the time of your detention?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have P1444 next. You were shown this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just then not to be broadcasted. Should we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you resided in Srebrenica, you said that you worked the land. Is it true that the land you worked on belonged to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that Serb still in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Srebrenica, were there any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few. And they were looking for a way out. I don't know whether they evacuated by themselves or if they were evacuated by the Red Cross though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the fate of the Serbs who lived in Srebrenica municipality; for example in the villages of Brezani, Turije, Tegari, Ratkovici, Fakovici, Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that happened before my village fell and before I arrived in Srebrenica. I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when you were in Srebrenica, in the villages I just mentioned, there were no longer any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I don't know. As for the town of Srebrenica and the land where we planted our crops, I didn't go further afield. I really don't know. Even today I don't know where Fakovici or Brezani or Turije is. If you believe me, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you stood guard at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my village where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While in military service, what weapon were you issued with?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an RBN.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if hand-held rocket-launchers existed in Srebrenica and who used them at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you have a witness from Srebrenica, you ask them. When I arrived I didn't have any weapons. Nobody ever asked them about weapons. We were not in a position to see any weapons, so I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you've been making comments and this is the first time this morning. I ask you to please stop that, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. These were all the questions that I had prepared for you.

utterances.speaker: RM297 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before you sit down, Mr. Lukic. Yesterday you attempted to tender 1D961. And then because you then wanted to tendered it with its attachments, and this witness could not answer any question from the attachments you ended up not doing anything about it. Are you not tendering 961? The photo only, not the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that in that attachment he confirmed there is Albanian woman, Elfete Veseli, who killed that guy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll have to refer me to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I think once you've found the transcript you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, can we MFI it then and I can come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would just put my objection at this point on the record not to the photograph which he identified but to the attached article. I think the witness gave all of the information that he had personal knowledge of and the article contains -- it's a lengthy article of information that he did not attest or affirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my recollection, and that's why I'm asking Mr. Lukic to tell us where the witness testified on the attachments. My recollection says he didn't say a word about the attachments. In fact, you didn't ask him questions, because you got an objection. When you tried to ask the questions you got an objection and then you moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I try to clarify that with the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I think you've got to go back to the transcript of yesterday. And for now the Chamber is prepared to admitted 1D961, and you can deal with the attachments once you have found the transcript for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you're ready, Madam Registrar, you may give a number to 1D961 without its attachments and the document is admitted into evidence. And maybe, Mr. Lukic, I suppose you will have to upload this [indiscernible] separately then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Once uploaded, document 1D961 receives number D284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I found the transcript reference from yesterday. Only it's temporary transcript. We only temporary transcript in the courtroom. It's page 43, line 13. I asked him about Elfete Veseli, last name is spelled correctly, and the witness confirmed, "That's what I heard."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything about the attachments. It talks about the person you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that person is mentioned in that attachment, in that text, newspaper text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And what does the newspaper text say -- support, if he says he heard about the person? He hasn't read the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not the first time here that we admit documents witness has never saw before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has no connection with the document. He has connection with what he heard about the person who was -- happens to be in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I think we have enough in the transcript, so it's not necessary for us to have that article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will upload only the picture then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Madam Hochhauser, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness RM297, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony for today. Thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify. You are now excused. Please travel safely back home. May the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Hochhauser, before I give you leave to leave, whereas you did mention it in your Prosecution filing somewhere that you may not tender 65 ter 15266 [Realtime transcript read in error "12566"], would you like to formally withdraw it from your 65 ter list now that it was not used with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we could do that. I don't anticipate using that sketch with any other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. It is so withdrawn, Madam Registrar. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has asked that I ask permission for him to be excused as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, through your counsel you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry. I notice also the transcript picked up the 65 ter number as "12566."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's "12566." Thank you. I now hand over to Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Moloto. Mr. Weber, you're the one remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, out of process of elimination. Good morning. At this time the Prosecution will call Mile Janjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I don't know if Your Honours are aware but we did send a brief communication last night that this witness has been previously [indiscernible] Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And then meanwhile I will use the time to deliver a decision in open session, but I do not know whether it has been provided to the booth so perhaps I wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booths have not been provided with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait until the decision has been distributed. Good morning, Mr. Janjic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janjic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: My name is Mile Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to deviate already, but I do not know if the Chamber wanted to admonish this witness or caution the witness at all before I proceed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's best to do now. Mr. Janjic, if any question will be put to you where a truthful answer would expose you to -- to reveal any criminal conduct by yourself, then please do not answer that question right away but first address the Chamber. We'll then decide whether or not you have to answer that question. Now, if we would put you under an obligation to answer that question, those answers could not be used in any proceedings before this Tribunal against you. But if there's any risk, please tell us openly that the answer might incriminate yourself. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, have you previously appeared before this Tribunal and provided testimony on three earlier occasions in the case of Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic as a Defence witness and in the Popovic and Tolimir cases as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you been informed that portions from your previous testimony in the Blagojevic and Popovic cases would be tendered as your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony here today, did you have an opportunity to review your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any clarifications or corrections to your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions, would you provide the same answers in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration in this case, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders at this time 65 ter numbers 28876, 28877, and 5183. 65 ter 28876 is the proffered transcript from the Blagojevic case; 65 ter 28877 is the proffered transcript from the Popovic case; there's one associated exhibit, 65 ter 5183, which is a photo discussed by the witness at Popovic transcript pages 17940 to 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think approximately 70 pages of transcript, that is not exactly within our guidance, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be the Prosecution's position that the approach with this witness is consistent with the general concept behind the guidance, although not specifically in accordance with the tendering of an amalgamated statement. As Your Honours have heard, this witness was initially appeared as a Defence witness. The best available and clearest record of his evidence so far has been his direct examination which is essentially chronological in the Blagojevic case. As Your Honours might be aware from our submission, there's a total of 251 pages of previous evidence that this witness has given and we have dramatically cut that down to 74 pages total, of what is directly and centrally relevant in this case and also reduced the number of associated exhibits to one that we're tendering. With respect to the evidence of the witness, he has been cautioned pursuant to Rule 90(E). He was originally a Defence witness. We have had minimal contact with him throughout the years and put his evidence on pursuant to Rule 92 ter on two previous occasions, which has been accepted, and then it has also been accepted on a third occasion pursuant to Rule 92 bis in the Karadzic case. So we are very cognizant of the Chamber's guidance, and we ask that this transcript be admitted at this time because it is, in our view, in accordance with the Chamber's general guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further comments -- or Mr. Stojanovic, any further comments? Certainly the fact that the witness originally was a Defence witness makes this situation slightly different from what we usually find.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct, Your Honours, that in the Blagojevic/Jokic case this witness was a Defence witness. We know that, and we will not object to the shortened version of the transcript be admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it then also not against the -- no objection against the associated exhibit which is only one. Madam Registrar, could you please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28876 receives number P1445. Document 28877 receives number P1446. And document 5183 receives number P1447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1445 up to and including -- 1445. P1445 up to and including 1447 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed with a presentation of a summary of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Mile Janjic was a member of the Bratunac military police in July 1995. The witness provides evidence of events that occurred at multiple locations between the 11th and 15th of July. On 11 July 1995, Mr. Janjic was tasked with providing security along the Sase-Pribicevac road. That evening, he returned to Bratunac and went to the Hotel Fontana where he and other Bratunac MPs were met by men who introduced themselves as the personal security detail of General Mladic. During the night of the 11th, the witness provided security both outside and inside the Hotel Fontana. On the morning of 12 July, Momir Nikolic told the witness and other Bratunac MPs to follow the orders of Colonel Jankovic. Subsequently, Colonel Jankovic ordered Mr. Janjic to count the number of people getting on buses and trucks in Potocari. Mr. Janjic counted the individuals boarding the buses on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995, and reported his numbers to Colonel Jankovic on both days. The witness also provides evidence about the separation of men and the military staff that he saw on those days in Potocari, including Generals Mladic and Krstic. Mr. Janjic provides further evidence that on the 14th or 15th of July, he was among several Bratunac MPs who went to a school in Rocevic. There, he saw 10 to 15 soldiers in a meadow near the school whom he recognised as being members of the Bratunac Brigade from Zenica. That concludes the summary of the witness. May the Prosecution proceed with further questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, before discussing some of the events between the 11th and the 15th of July, the Prosecution would like to ask you an additional question concerning a photo that's already been admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 43 of Exhibit P1155, and we request if the Court Officer could please magnify the photo on this page. If we could have just the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, on pages 9772 to -73 of your previous testimony in the Blagojevic case, you identified yourself as being the individual depicted at number 1, and General Krstic being the individual at number 2. My question to you is following: Did you see General Krstic in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995 or on only one of those days?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I saw him on one of those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that was the first day you were in Potocari or the second day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, one of those days. I believe it was on day one, but that I'm not 100 per cent sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're done with the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the evening of 11 July 1995, during your previous testimony in the Blagojevic case, at pages 9759 to -60, you stated: "In front of the hotel, we were met by men who introduced themselves as the personal security detail of General Mladic, and they gave us these certain tasks." Could you please tell us how many men you were met by?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There were three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they had camouflage overalls; i.e., they were wearing uniforms belonging to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On pages 9760 and -61 of your previous testimony in Blagojevic, you discuss how you were one of the Bratunac MPs who provided security on the exterior and interior of the Hotel Fontana between the evening of the 11th and morning of the 12th. Did you see General Mladic at any point in time while you were providing the security?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Only once. On the 11th, in the evening, I saw him in front of the reception desk as he was walking in the direction of the restaurant within the hotel. I did not see him from very close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you see him on any other occasions after that evening?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly on the following morning, on the 12th that is. It was very early in the morning when I saw him. It was on the 13th -- no, it was on the 12th; I apologise. He was on the first floor of the Hotel Fontana. I suppose that he had just left the room where he had spent that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were you specifically when you saw him on this -- following morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: One of my tasks besides providing security for the Fontana hotel was to patrol at the reception on the ground floor. From the ground floor a staircase leads to the first floor. There were a couple of us or perhaps three of us, and at the beginning of that hallway or at the end of the staircase, that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before discussing your counting of individuals on the 12th and 13th in Potocari, I'd like to ask you a few general questions about the separation of men and women on these days. Could you please briefly explain to us the process used to separate the men from the women in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In front of that group of people consisting of the inhabitants of Srebrenica, there was a red and yellow police ribbon. There were UNPROFOR soldiers in front of that ribbon and there were also members of the special police. When buses, lorries, and other vehicles arrived, somebody would lift that ribbon and they would let groups of people of perhaps 100 or 200 people, i.e., larger groups of people, towards the buses. The buses, lorries, and other vehicles were parked some 80 to 100 metres in the direction of Bratunac from that ribbon. That group of people would walk the distance of some 80 to 100 metres, and on their way, on the left and the right-hand side of the asphalt road leading from Srebrenica to Bratunac, members of the special police were lined up. And while the group was moving in the direction of the buses, the males were directed towards the left side of the road looking towards Srebrenica, then they were directed on an adjacent road towards a house on the left-hand side of the Srebrenica-Bratunac road. At the same time, the women and the children would go on walking to the right and they would get on the buses that were parked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your answer, you just mentioned a house. What colour was that house, and could you give us a better description of the building that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can explain the location itself. The house itself was white, so nothing out of the ordinary. What I could observe, that it had a large yard which reached up to the asphalt road and the canal, that is to say, the main road between Srebrenica and Bratunac. It was to the left of the road from Srebrenica to Bratunac, and that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After or during the separation process on the 12th or the 13th, were you able to see where the men were taken before they were boarded onto buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I said, they were in the yard. I saw them in the yard of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your Blagojevic testimony, on page 9828, you were asked whether you heard any women crying during the course of the separations. Your answer was yes. Did you hear women crying on both the 12th and 13th of July during the course of the separations?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did this crying continue throughout both days?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said yes. As for this last question, I can't really answer because I truly don't remember. I don't remember how long it lasted and whether it was throughout the two days. There were women crying and protesting, but I can't say how long it all lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your previous testimony before the Tribunal, you've explained the counting of men and women who boarded buses and trucks on the 12th and 13th in Potocari. Today I would like to focus specifically with you on the number of men who were placed on the buses on these dates. Starting with the number of men on the 12th of July, I'm going to review your previous testimony and ask you to clarify your answers. In your Blagojevic testimony, at page 9844, you explained that on the first day, there were between 10 and 15 buses with men, and you indicated there were over 50 men per bus. In your Popovic testimony, at page 17942, you were asked whether you could give any better estimate of the number of men per bus. You indicated it was over 50 people, most likely 70. You continued to explain your sampling method and stated on page 17943: "But I stand by the numbers concerning the buses. It was 70 and not 50." Could you please confirm for us whether I understand correctly that on the 12th of July, there were between 10 and 15 buses loaded with men and there were approximately 70 men per bus, according to your sampling method.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes, and I can clarify the discrepancy between the two statements. There is a small difference because the sample I relied on was based on the number of women and children on the 12th in the morning. I did not count the men, and I thought at a certain point, I thought that there should have been less than 70. However, if we look at the number of bodies, or actually, the size of the bodies and the difference between men and women, one would think that more women could fit into a single bus. However, my assumption was not confirmed because even though children and women were somewhat smaller, the women had items with them, packages, et cetera. So, in my view, the figure could have been between 50 and 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the number of men on the 13th. In the Popovic case, on page 17945, you estimated that there were "certainly two or three times more" from the previous day. What do you base this estimate upon?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The difference between the first and the second day consisted in the following: The first day, in the morning, the people left on those ten buses or so. On the second day, as of noon onwards, they began leaving together with the rest. The women and the men were being boarded onto the buses as well, and they did not have to wait until the end of that day, like the first day. So the yard was already full before the first departure. Since it was full, they were sent further afield from the road which was to the left of the Srebrenica-Bratunac road. Right past the house, there's a meadow on the left-hand side, the same side where the house is, and that's where they were sent. It is some 50 to 100 metres away from the house. There was a large group of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And on the second day, did you use the same counting method as the first day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The same method, yes. However, the difference on the second day was that the men were no longer transported on buses. They were also being transported on truck, much like the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to one of your earlier answers, and you refer to the fact that the women had items with them, packages, et cetera. This is on page -- page 22, lines 22 and 23. Did the men have any packages with them?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it might be time for a break. If this is a suitable moment for a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll take a break of 20 minutes. Could you please follow the usher, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, Mr. Weber, I do understand that the parties will make a great effort to see whether we can conclude the evidence of this witness today. How much time would you still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't be long. Maybe 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's see whether we can conclude the testimony of this witness today. Mr. Stojanovic, any -- We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, during your previous testimonies, you've explained your interactions with Colonel Jankovic on the 12th and 13th of July in Potocari. During your Blagojevic testimony, at page 9768, you were asked: "Could you please tell us who was your commanding officer to your understanding?" You answered: "Well, as I understood at the moment, and in view of rank, it was Colonel Jankovic." Were you under the command of Colonel Jankovic on both the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was in my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Why was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Because Major Nikolic, Momir Nikolic, who was a major at the time, sent me to an officer who was senior to him, who was a colonel, to be at his disposal, and I was at his disposal for the two days; that is to say, from the morning till evening, not during the night though. In my understanding, I was under his command for the two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 9788 of your Blagojevic testimony, in reference to events on the 12th of July, you indicated that the reports or numbers came in in instalments throughout the day, and Colonel Jankovic was the one who was supposed to do the adding up? Did you provide periodic reports of the number of people who were placed on the buses and trucks to Colonel Jankovic on the 13th of July also?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The question is somewhat unclear. Since there were reports coming intermittently -- well, I don't think such reports were arriving from elsewhere. It was me, instead, who reported the figures to Colonel Jankovic on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you provide the reports on both the 12th and 13th to Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On a few occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would -- when you say "on a few occasions," could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I will explain it the following way: I explained how I counted for the first hours on the 12th. And, after that, I explained how it came that the colonel accepted this idea on how to take samples of the people boarded onto the vehicles. On several occasions, since I realised that there was another person who was counting the number of people leaving Srebrenica, several times we were in contact with Colonel Jankovic. On one such occasion, he told me and the other person from the civilian police to count more carefully in order to have at least approximate figures. So he had both of us in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Jankovic the only person you were reporting these figures to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Colonel Jankovic communicated any information about your number counts to members of any international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that kind of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you the only Bratunac MP involved in the counting of individuals in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: For the first few hours of the 12th, the answer is no. There were several members of the MP platoon involved. After the first two to three hours on the 12th, I was the only person doing so. When we reverted to the sample-taking procedure, then I remained as the only person counting the trucks and buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the names of the other Bratunac MPs who participated in the counting on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can recall a couple for the first two to three hours: Milovan Mitrovic, Milan Gvozdenovic, Zdravko Ilic, myself, Zoran Zivanovic, and perhaps someone else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We missed the first name. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last two were Zdravko Ilic and Zoran Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first name that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Radenko Zaric, Milovan Mitrovic. I mentioned the two of them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you or Milan Gvozdenovic receive any specific orders or tasks during the evening of 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what Colonel Jankovic ordered you both to do?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: First, he asked if we had a vehicle at our disposal. Since we answered positively, he ordered that we get into the vehicle, since the ribbon had been removed by that time, and since we could not see any further afield from where we were standing, there were no more -- no more inhabitants there. He told us to drive in the direction of Srebrenica, deeper inside the territory, and in case we encountered more civilians en route, to tell them to go to Potocari and wait and that, the next day, transport would be organised and that they would be all be driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you carry out this order?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to change topics a little bit. On page 17950 to -51 of your Popovic testimony, you discuss what you saw when you went to Rocevic on the 14th or 15th of July. You indicated that you saw a few of your colleagues and a group of 10 to 15 soldiers of the Serbian army outside of a school in what you described as a yard or meadow close to that building. Do you recall this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you interact with any of your colleagues or the other Serbian soldiers when you saw them near the school in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe this interaction.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I believe I said so a number of times before. I didn't know why we went to Rocevic and what our task was to be there. We were there for a brief period only. I got off the vehicle, when we arrived in front of a school. This is where I encountered the group of soldiers. There was even a colleague, a work-mate from the military police. Out of curiosity I asked them what they were doing there and what was going on. They said, although I couldn't see it, that there were men inside the school, Muslim men, and that they were brought there. To their knowledge, they were supposed to have been transported in the direction of Teocak. I heard of that location. It is somewhere between Tuzla and Zvornik, although I have never visited the place. That's all I could learn from the colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 191 of 65 ter 5248.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, while the next exhibit is coming up, if you could tell us who from the Bratunac military police was present when you saw them near the school.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Who was present in front of the school or in general? Because I did mention that a number of vehicles arrived. Do you mean the people whom we met in front of the school or the people who arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were there any Bratunac MPs in front of the school; and, if so, could you tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I met a work-mate of mine whose name is Zoran Zivanovic and we had a brief conversation. I was also present when he talked to Mirko Jankovic, the MP platoon commander, so I have to mention that he was there as well. He wasn't in front of the school but outside the yard. He was there with an APC of the UN which was painted white.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So we have it clearly on the record in this case, do I understand correctly that Milenko Jankovic is a different person than Colonel Jankovic who you reported to on the 12th and 13th of July? I'm sorry, that was Mirko Jankovic. That was my mistake. Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a different person. Mirko Jankovic was the MP platoon commander in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I seek clarification of one of the areas. It may be a translation or a language matter. Witness, you were recorded as having said the following. You were talking about men "inside the school, Muslim men, and that they were brought there. To their knowledge, they were supposed," and now you're talking about the men with whom you had a conversation, "to their knowledge, they were supposed to have been transported in the direction of Teocak." I have difficulties in understanding that they were supposed to have been transported. Is it that they were supposed to be transported in that direction? Or is it that they had already been transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is correct. They were supposed to be transported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, I'd just like to direct your attention to the photograph that's before you. Do you recognise what is depicted?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This building looks like the school in Rocevici. I'm a bit confused by the fence in front of it. I don't remember it looking like that. But I do remember that this was the backyard. The gym was on the left-hand side. The ground floor and the first floor remind me a lot of that school and the road in front of the school. And you can see the gate in the photo, the electrical posts, and the fence, and can you see the road that is below the school, and that is the Zvornik-Bijeljina road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would tender this single photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs to be uploaded as a single photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Ms. Stewart also just reminded me of the same. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we already assign a number to it. Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Once uploaded the photo will receive number P1448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you please inform Madam Registrar once -- once it is uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Janjic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to take into account what you have told us so far. I'll use some photos, video-clips, and documents to jog your memory and I will have some questions for you. The first one being: When did you join the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I joined the military police sometime in the summer of 1994. It was either in June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that that was a unit that would match an infantry platoon in strength and that's exactly how you were organised?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I will agree that it had up to 50 men at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In military terms, who were you directly subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we were supposed to be subordinated to the brigade commander. However, in factual terms one could easily say that we received all of our orders from Major Momir Nikolic. He seems to have been in charge of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the seat of the military police platoon with regard to the command of the Bratunac Brigade? Physically, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the entrance into the building that housed the Bratunac Brigade. There were a few small buildings there, and our buildings -- building was perhaps 30 to 40 metres from the building where the Bratunac Brigade was billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade kept records of the duty service and that the records were kept daily, covering the activities of your platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to see that log-book that was kept at the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to call up 65 ter 04205. Let us look at page 12 in B/C/S and page 9 in English. Mr. Janjic, this is one of the pages that I would like to show you and invite your comments. In the left upper corner, it says that this was recorded on the 8th of July, 1995. Can you see that? Look at the left-hand side upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, here, in the central part of that page, it says that on the 8th of July, during the shift military conscripts were brought in and that there was a patrol working at check-points, and there's something that I would like to concentrate on. A patrol consisting of four military policemen went to Pribicevac for UNPROFOR members. Can you remember what happened exactly? Were you a member of that patrol?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can state for a fact that I was not a member of that patrol but apart from that, I really can't remember what this was about. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I make a little pause, please don't hold it against me. I'm waiting for the interpretation to be over. Do you know that there came a time in Bratunac when a group of UNPROFOR members appeared and that they were billeted there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then let's look at the same document, but this time I'm looking at page 15 in B/C/S, and in English it would be on page 12. Let's wait for the English version. Thank you. This is another page in that log-book. It covers the date of the 11th of July. And, to the best of your recollection and according to your testimony, you provided security for the Pribicevac-Spat road, or Pribicevac-Sase road.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would call it the Sase-Pribicevac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that one group of the military police provided security for the Pribicevac-Spat road to protect Ratko Mladic and others. First of all, can you tell us what the toponym "Spat" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was never there. There is a place called Spat; I remember that from war time. It is a small village, I suppose, but I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that village close to the Sase-Pribicevac road?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is closer to Pribicevac, but I don't want to speculate. I'm sure that it is in the Pribicevac sector, but I would only be -- speculated if I attempted to tell you exactly where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On that day, as so many times before or during the month of July, we're talking a period of seven or five days, we provided security along the road. We were told that a large group of officers were taking that road on their way to Pribicevac and that our task was to provide security for their safe passage, for their safe return as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time there was a forward command post in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There was a command post of the 3rd Battalion in Pribicevac. It had been set up much before. I believe that it was set up in 1993, if not even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point on the 11 July, General Ratko Mladic also took that road in his vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber when it was, when that vehicle drove by.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can't say when that happened, when the vehicle was travelling towards Pribicevac. I only knew that the general was travelling towards Pribicevac on that day, that we had to exert more caution. I saw that vehicle on its way back in late afternoon. I believe that it was after 5.00. I'm sure that it was not before 5.00. It was after 5.00, but I don't know whether it was around 6.00 or around 7.00. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that vehicle moving towards Srebrenica or from Srebrenica at the moment when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I've just told you, that vehicle was returning from Pribicevac, and that could only be in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you take another route from Pribicevac to get to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I assume that that would be the case, but I don't know. It's only my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, in the vicinity of the place where you were, there was a NATO air strike; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That happened on the 11th, much before General Mladic returned. We knew that he was in the Pribicevac sector which increased our concern. NATO aircraft were observed, and we were close to the command post, which is a bit lower, and I believe that their sortees inflicted more -- damaged on us, who were above Pribicevac. Some 2- or 300 metres from our vehicles there were two aircrafts flying over us. They were throwing cluster bombs or something like that. We heard a lot of explosions. They must have thrown dozens or hundreds of those bombs. We were powerless there. All we had was a Pinzgauer vehicle. At that moment I was in the vehicle. I opened fire from the anti-aircraft gun without any success. There were a few more sortees. They threw their load on our positions and they vanished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, when did that happen on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say that that happened in the afternoon after 12.00 but much before the time when General Ratko Mladic returned -- was returning from Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, the place where those bombs landed, as you called them, how far was that from Pribicevac, i.e., from the command post?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to be precise. The closest to us was perhaps 200 to 300 metres. And looking from the command post, it could have perhaps been 500 metres, or even up to 1 kilometre away from that place. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the vehicle that passed you by and you were told that it was general -- General Mladic's vehicle in that convoy, but you didn't see General Mladic himself, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was standing perhaps 20 to 30 metres away, and I could see what I could see. But my colleague who was closer to the road than I was - Nenad Jokic was his name - was very close to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How much later after General Mladic went by did you stay in the field; and when did you receive your new orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We stayed on for a very short time. According to experience, we knew that after the high-ranking officers passed by, we would be called off and then we would be repositioned. Very shortly after that, and it was a customary practice, like so many times before that, we gathered. We got into the vehicles and we headed for the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the next order that you received on -- late in the afternoon on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Our next order, as soon as we arrived, we did not even park our vehicles properly in front of the military police premises at the gate of the premises of the Bratunac Brigade. Our vehicle was stopped by our colleagues, police officers whose name I don't remember, and we were given a task to urgently go in the direction of Pobrdze and to bring Ljubisav Simic, Professor Simic. I know that he had to do about the municipality. He was either president or something-like that. Another group of police officers that were standing next to us were given a task to bring Miroslav Deronjic. They went to his house on foot. He resided very close to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. During that period of time, he also discharged some duties in the municipality. I really don't know which one of them was what but I know that they were both highly positioned in the civilian authorities in the municipality. And let me just emphasise that within the perimeter of the Bratunac Brigade command, i.e., in front of the building closer to the gate, we saw a large number of officers, I could spot them during that brief period of time, and I could see that General Mladic was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who gave you your order?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I've just told you, our colleagues from the police turned up. I can't remember who they were. I don't know who gave us that particular order. I know who gave us our next order after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that evening, you brought Mr. Ljubisav Simic with you, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did not bring Ljubisav Simic. I knew where his house was. We came in front of the house. We rang the bell. His wife opened the door. And I believed her when she told me. She used to be my Russian language teacher in high school, so we believed her. We did not enter the house. We did not search the house. I believed her when she told us that Mr. Simic was away on business in Montenegro. That's why we did not bring him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what we heard. And then when you returned, did you receive a new order?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic approached us. There were several of us there, and he told us to go in the direction of the Fontana hotel, because our next order had to do with the hotel. This is what we did after having spent a very short time in the military police building. We stayed there perhaps 15 minutes to half an hour. A group of some 15 police officers on foot set out in the direction of Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task in front of the hotel? What were you supposed to do there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We were told that everything would become clear when we got there. When we arrived in front of the hotel, we were approached by uniformed soldiers. They introduced themselves as the personal detail of General Mladic, and they explained to us that some negotiations were to take place there and that our task was to provide security for the -- the general sector of the Fontana hotel. At that time, the area around the hotel was not a pedestrian area so we were supposed to stop the traffic and to remove all the civilians. We were deployed there, and we carried out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you go on performing that task on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We stayed there until the early morning hours of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at one point in time an UNPROFOR delegation arrived in the hotel from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I remember that their vehicles arrived. They were quite striking. They parked in front of the restaurant. There's a parking lot there that can accommodate up to 10 vehicles. It is actually a garden terrace belonging to the hotel. They parked very close to the entrance. It was already dark; I don't know how late it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were there any other activities that evening? Did anybody else arrive? Did anyone leave? Were there any other vehicles that arrived? Or did some vehicles leave?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can be sure of that one time. I can't remember any other arrivals. We were tasked with providing security for a large area around the hotel so I was not there all the time. There were times when -- times when I was behind the hotel and not very close to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anything that might indicate that somebody was slaughtering a pig, either in front of the hotel or behind the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a lot of noise -- a slaughtering pig produces a lot of noise, and if that was happening close to the hotel and in view of where you were positioned, would you have been able to hear such a noise?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I would have heard it. Maybe I didn't say this, but I would like to say now that we had a short intervention. In the close vicinity of the hotel, we could hear music coming out of the house. I believe that the house belonged to the Ilic family. I knew them. I went to school there, so I knew a lot of people, and we went there and asked them to turn the music down. That house is across the street from the hotel, some 200 metres from the hotel. That music was quite audible. It was quite loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Could the witness -- do you -- do you understand the English language, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. I'm wondering, Mr. Stojanovic, what is the position of the Defence, because earlier we -- when witnesses testified about the slaughtering of a pig, we were presented with a document which: I gave permission to slaughter a pig. Now it seems now your line of questioning to be that no pig was ever slaughtered, so that confuses me slightly. Is the position of the Defence that there was a -- if I could say so, a regular slaughtering of a pig not intended to intimidate, or is the position of the Defence there was no slaughtering of a pig at all? Could you tell us what position of the Defence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of this Defence after the consultations with the client is clear. No pig was slaughtered. There was no intimidation of that kind. Let me just finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe the language spoken might be something that could be understood by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have thought about that. But I think it's -- it's not dramatic at this moment. So finally your position is that, despite -- so we do have to understand that the permission to do it was -- is then going against your own case or ... I'm just wondering what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw a document from the Tolimir case which was an approval and that approval is not in dispute. But that activity did not take place in front of the hotel at the time that was indicated here. Our client -- and we will hear that from other witnesses as well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't say that that document was presented in relation to any event that took place beyond hearing distance from the witness at that time. But let's leave it to that. This witness has told us now that he didn't hear any such thing of a kind. So let's move on before we enter up into too many details. And if I could give you some guidance, this witness gives quite a lot of details which seems to be not that relevant for his story, so if you could please keep tight control over questions and answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since -- I may put one short question. Now the witness has his earphones on again. We have still the -- this page of the log-book of Bratunac Brigade in front of us on the screen. I would only want to -- I'd like to put one question to the witness. We see on the bottom of that page, and you see it as well, two names: One name is Bozic; the next is Nikolic. Above that, there is one single word. Could you explain that word? I ask because it's not reflected in the English translation. What is written there and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the name. It seems German to me. In any case, it reads Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Above the name -- above that name, Bozic, what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Ona nama is Bozic." That is the sentence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Judge is asking you about the B/C/S document in our language.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't have it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a word in the B/C/S text that is missing from the English text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness says "I don't have it in B/C/S." We first have to verify whether the witness receives this document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's gone from our screens too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the document in B/C/S? That is, in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is written just above the two names? It seems to be one word --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems someone's assisting me. It says "prijavnica [phoen]" which could be gatehouse or a reception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- I don't know whether the document will be tendered, but if so, the Chamber would like to have a complete translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will of course take care to correct the translation. Our position would be that the 65 ter should be made in whole, rather brief log of the July [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but whatever, long or short, we would like to have a complete translation that's [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of course, I just want to know because we will check the other pages too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the 12th of July now and Potocari. Did you have any knowledge as to who Colonel Jankovic was?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Not until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you discussed the process of separation for men and mentioned the members of this special brigade of the police, how did you know that they were the people separating the men from the group of refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I knew it because they had introduced themselves to me in a conversation. When I talked to them, I learned who they were, what unit they belonged to, and when they said that they were "specials," that is to say the special police, I knew then what kind of people they were and how they were assembled. After I learned who they were, and after I remembered what their uniforms -- uniforms looked like, I could see them as well engaging in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You, however, did not take part in the separation activity of separating the able-bodied men from the rest.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, not at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see any member of the Bratunac Brigade taking part in the process.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't -- or, rather, I couldn't see members of the Bratunac Brigade there because they weren't there. I explained in detail that at first there were some 15 MPs there who belonged to the Bratunac Brigade. Amp that the number went down to six or seven and at certain points in time there were even less of us present in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will rephrase my question. Did you see any member of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade on the 12th of July at any point in time taking part in the separation of able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything you saw regarding the separation process, when the able-bodied men were separated, was that members of the special police brigade engaged in it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And I have explained already the -- the process itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you the following: At some point in time, you saw General Mladic arrive, as you explained, in Potocari. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see General Mladic at some point address the refugees in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I saw him go there. I saw him move in that direction. He didn't stay there for long, and I can only suppose that he addressed them because I couldn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at excerpt from those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P1147, the video we've used already. The segment I'm interested in begins at 24:40 ending at 25:42. After that, I will have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we take some patience until we see and hear anything. If you do the same, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, do you remember whether General Mladic arrived in Potocari before the transport set out, or at the moment people began being transported?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot be certain. I can say that I saw him twice, and I'm positive. When he arrived, he was stopped by the group of people where this footage was shot. It was some 120 metres away. I mentioned the distribution of food and that he was shouting at members of the logistic battalion. So he stayed there for a brief period. Then he passed by the place where I was. I was 100 metres away from the group. He was accompanied by some security officers. He went to the ribbon and went back. In the course of those couple of days I saw him one other time. I know that he went in the direction of Vijogor because the people from the MP platoon, my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I'll get to that because I think it is an important fact, but for the time being kindly answer only the questions that I have put to you so we can conclude today. The other thing that I wanted to ask you about: You said that you saw General Mladic at some point shout at members of the logistics battalion. What was it all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it will take time. I've tried already to explain it in detail. We spent those two days without food or water. What I could observe after his departure was that we saw a vehicle packed with food and water, and they were distributing it to the people to the side of the road, the people on the buses, and everywhere else. We, as the military policemen also tried to get some food because our supply did not work. The same was done by the members of the special police, but we were turned away. We were told that it was Mladic's orders, that he was shouting at them, and that all the food and water was to go to the people leaving. This is what remains etched in my memory. We hoped to get something from the forces of UNPROFOR, and it was incomprehensible to me because we knew that after we entered they had tens of tonnes of food and water and yet they distributed perhaps a few litres of water and I didn't see a single loaf of bread in circulation. I never seen them distribute anything to the population there. After all of it, we took over the camp securing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that too, but let's stop here for now. Did I understand you well that you received information that it was General Mladic's order to give the food and water to the refugees and not to the soldiers and policemen from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break in a second. But I'd like to ask one clarifying question. You said that UNPROFOR had tens of tonnes of food and water. What's the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to clarify but I was interrupted by counsel. What I tried to say is the following: After all of the events, a few days later, after the 12th and the 13th, let's say, between the 15th and the 20th, I claim it responsibly, our next task, the task of the MP platoon, was to secure -- well, the UNPROFOR soldiers had left by then. We had to secure the base so that their property would not be taken away and looted. So we were there at least or over seven days, maybe ten days to a fortnight. At the time, military vehicles came from the VRS, and they took truck -- it took truck upon truck for them to take away the food and fuel. The containers were towed away as well, where they were billeted, where they slept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you found -- at least the trucks that transported fuel and food out, found all those tens of tonnes of food and fuel in the premises of UNPROFOR after the 15th. Is that the source of your knowledge? Did you see it, or did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I was present because I, too, provided security then. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you saw it. That was my question. Could you please follow the usher because we'll take a break. Mr. Stojanovic, we are on track, in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will conclude even sooner. So, in any case, we'll conclude today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time. The Chamber was informed by the Office of the Prosecution that the photograph, which is page 191 of the 65 ter document 5248, that single page that had been tendered today and assigned provisionally Exhibit P1448, has been uploaded separately as 65 ter P5248B, and P1448 is therefore now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I put the question, I would like to say that 1D961 has been uploaded as a photo, and it bears number D284. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] this is confirmed by Madam Registrar, and it has been accordingly now been corrected in e-court so that everything now is accurate in the records of this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will continue talking about the 12th of July. Kindly tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your recollection, we saw a clip depicting General Mladic. Where was that taken? In what area? What are the facilities behind him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I managed to recognise the population behind and the strikingly remarkable red-and-white ribbon which was an imaginary boundary. That would be lifted up and people that were behind that ribbon would be let through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your estimate how far was that from the facility where the men were accommodated after having been separated from the women and children?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: About 100 metres, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at another clip together. I would like us to look at P1147 from 28:08 to 28:44. I'm going to show you just a frozen photo taken from that clip. After you see it, I will have a few questions for -- for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this a clip that were -- was shown to you during the examination-in-chief and did you recognise yourself in that clip?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because I could see myself again coming from the background and looking in the direction of the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General Krstic provided this statement and repeated General Mladic's words, according to which the population would be transported if they so wished. Do you remember that you heard General Krstic saying anything else, in addition to what was recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I was not in a position to hear -- hear what I can hear in the clip. I came from the background. I realised that he was being interviewed. I may have caught a few words. I couldn't really hear them. I can't remember that I saw General Krstic providing any orders and instructions or saying anything to anybody else. And I repeat: I did not hear, at the time, what I can hear now in the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
