utterances.text: We're talking about the 12th of July, day one of your stay in Potocari. Did you ever see any ill-treatment, abuse against the refugees in the area? Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, none of that. General Mladic was there. I saw him on several occasions, and I must say that the level of discipline was really very high, at a very enviable level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The place where you were when this video was recorded and General Krstic's statement, how far was that from the place where General Mladic's statement was recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you take a better look, you will see those buses in the background, and we know that those buses were some 80 metres away from the place where we saw General Mladic before. So the distance was certainly 80 metres if not more. I already told you how far the buses were from the imaginary boundary marked with that red-and-white ribbon. It must have been at least 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to call up P61 which an is aerial photo of the Potocari sector as it was on the 12th of July. And then I will ask the witness to take a pencil, or a pen, rather, and to mark certain localities. Let's first wait for the document to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any reason to believe that -- I don't know what you want the witness to mark, but do you expect him to mark, for example, what was often called the white house in a different place? Or, I mean, I'm just wondering to what extent what you are about to do may be repetitious and to what extent it may not even be in dispute. Would you please keep that very much in mind when you ask the witness to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will certainly bear that in mind. Maybe that exercise will not even be necessary. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the photo. That photo was taken at 1400 hours on the 12th of the July. Could you please tell us whether you can see the place where General Mladic provided his statement, i.e., where you was interviewed for TV?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, and you know it very well because you showed me similar aerial photos in my previous testimony, I had a very hard time finding my bearings. The Judges helped me. I can testify orally. I can make markings, but I'm not very good at marking photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I had not insist, in that case. I know that that is exactly how it was. But now I would like you to pay attention to a question that you tried to elaborate in your answer but then I interrupted. At one point, on the 12th of July you say that you remember that one group of MP members received a different order and that was to head in the direction of Viogor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know what vehicle they took. I can give you the names of one or two of the policemen who went in the direction of Viogor. Their mission didn't stop there. After Viogor, according to what they told us later, they escorted General Mladic to Vlasenica and even further. I don't know how far. In any case, it was in the direction of Han Pijesak. Maybe they went even as far as Han Pijesak. This is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to elaborate on that. Tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your recollection, who were the military policemen who were told to go to Viogor and escort General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The Pinzgauer vehicle with an anti-aircraft machine-gun was driven by Milovan Mitrovic. I can also say with 100 per cent certainty that there was Zeljko Zaric there, as well as Mladen Blagojevic. I would stop there because I'm not sure about the others. I only know that there were two or three others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber when was it, on the 12th of July, when they were sent on that mission?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. I already told you that they returned late that night. I told you where they had been sent to. They returned quite late during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where the Viogor sector is in relation to Potocari. What is the distance between the two?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Bratunac, if you drive on the Bratunac-Srebrenica road, the road to Viogor forks off in the direction of Zepa on the right. You have to turn before Potocari, and it is certainly more than 4 or 5 kilometres away from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out at any point in time why General Mladic went to Viogor on that day in the afternoon? Did your colleagues tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: They told me, because the movement of the troops of the Bratunac Brigade and many other troops happened after Srebrenica was taken. The next mission was to go to Zepa, and there's just one road leading to Zepa, one may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After leaving the Potocari sector on the 12th of July, according to your recollection, did General Mladic ever return to that sector?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say yes or no because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that that patrol on that day went as far as Vlasenica and Han Pijesak. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those police officers, your colleagues, and you have told us three of their names, did they tell you that they escorted General Mladic all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they shared the detail with us. I -- I suppose that those details would be of no consequence for this Trial Chamber. But, yes, they did share their experiences and a lot of tiny details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask one other time-related question. Are you sure that that happened on the 12th in the afternoon, or is it perhaps possible that that happened on the 13th in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. You are insisting on the 12th, whereas, I have repeated on several occasions that I'm not sure about the dates. All the details are correct. Everything is accurate but the date. You were mention -- insisting on the date, and I -- I forget to mention that I'm really not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's focus now and let me hear from you whether it would be correct that General Mladic left for Viogor on the first day of your stay in Potocari, i.e., on the 12th of July. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would be speculating if I said that I'm sure. I told you when I saw him, where I saw him, how I saw him. I can only tell you with 100 per cent certainty that it was in the afternoon, but I would be speculating about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me ask you this: In methodological terms or in technical terms, how did you count the buses that drove men off from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I've already said several times that the same procedure applied to women, children, and men. We were counting women and children for the first couple of three hours on the 12th. And then on the 12th in the evening, there were some dozen buses with men and we counted all those men that left Potocari. And the same repeated on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's simplify. Did you count people or did you count buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: For the first three hours, I counted people on the 12th in the morning. Later on, we counted buses, lorries, and other similar vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that you started by counting heads, that you realised that it was a time-consuming exercise, and then you decided to count the number of vehicles that were taking people away. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes. But that was done with approval by Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point, Colonel Jankovic addressed the men in your vicinity, and he informed them about the procedure that would ensue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes, and that happened on the 12th in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear Colonel Jankovic say to these people when they asked him what would happen with them next?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He came across as sincere. He tried to calm them down. He told them there was no need for concern or panic, that the buses would arrive, that they would all be transported and that they would catch up with their families. They would be taken to the same destination as them and that there was no need for them to be afraid, to panic, or any such thing. That's what he told them, and I heard his words myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally at any point in time have any information that a lot of those people would be anything else but exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: What did you say? Exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said exchange. Did you believe that they would be exchanged? Did you take that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believed that, and I kept on believing that for a long time. But now I believe that a lot of them were killed. Whoever passes through Potocari, I can see a lot of graves. I understand that a lot of the people had been killed. I didn't know. I couldn't even suspect that something like that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The record of the number of people leaving Potocari was kept by an employee of the civilian police from the Bratunac police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court his name.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The person's name is Milisav Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The men who were separated on the 12th of July were taken away in a single group from Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in my assessment, there were between 10 and 15 buses," and we're talking about the first day, and if I understood properly there were no trucks that day, how is it possible then that if you kept record of the number of buses to have such a wide margin of differing answers as compared to the number of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My mistake. I'll reformulate. Tell me this: The number of buses which took away the separated able-bodied men, and you said there were between 10 and 15 vehicles, was it your assessment and that you are unaware of the exact figure?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That is why I put it within the range of between 10 to 15 buses. There may have been eight, or 13, or a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that is your free estimate, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It is my free estimate because I didn't try to commit to my memory the figures in any other way, so it's an assessment of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the 13th, but let me conclude the 12th first. Tell me this: When you were asked about seeing personal effects being on the ground in front of the facility where the able-bodied men were, did you see any passports strewn about belonging to those men?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As regards the personal possessions, many such questions were put to me at different times. I'm not a lawyer so I don't see what the point is, but I did try to clarify it in the Blagojevic trial. It is my opinion, and if we know that close-by there is a general of an army, I didn't see anything wrong with the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What the question is whether you saw any passports. Whether that's legally relevant or whether there is anything wrong in that is a different matter. Did you see passports there? That's the question. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see any passports. I saw a pile of things though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question. Tell us this next, please: To the best of your recollection when on the 12th of July did you leave the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Late -- in late afternoon, before dark. As was the case on the 13th. It was late in the afternoon. It was still daylight because it was summertime. So my guess is between 7.00 and 8.00 p.m. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Between 8.00 and 9.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the night between the 12th and the 13th there were any transports, or was all transportation halted during the night until the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, and I don't know. I don't think there was any because my task continued the next day; that is, do not [as interpreted] count the people. When I came there in the morning, I didn't see them and I wasn't there during the night so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The convoys of vehicles taking away the refugees had to go through the centre of Bratunac in order to reach Kladanj; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some members of the Bratunac Brigade MP platoon also secured the streets so as to have no problems with the evacuation when passing through the town?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There were some people there, and I can cite their names. They told me what they did and they said that they were securing the streets. That's my work-mates, policemen, told me later on. They said that they secured the outpatient clinic in Bratunac, that some women were in labour and people requiring medical assistance, and they also secured the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look together at a document from the duty log-book of the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade. And we'll comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter 04205 again, page 16 in the B/C/S and 13 in the English version of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Weber, I was rather critical about an incomplete translation. I meanwhile notice that the same name word either written in Cyrillic or in Latin script appears on almost every page and is always translated as "reception." So under those circumstances, the Chamber does not insist on having a lot of work done on that matter. Of course, if there are any other flaws, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay with you we'll just check it just to be sure [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but for that one page the word appears clearly and the lack of -- we have another 15 or 16 pages to see what that word means, and that is "reception."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. As on the present page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you. It is page 16 in the B/C/S and 13 in the English. Apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, again before us is a page of the log-book kept by the military police platoon pertaining to the 12th and 13th of July. It is stated that one part of the police force secured the sick and wounded in the clinic, as can you see in the middle of the passage in the B/C/S. Is this precisely what you told us about when you said that some military policemen secured the wounded and sick at the outpatient clinic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can see this document, but this is the first time that I see it. I mentioned that I know the names of people who told me about that. Milan Ilic told me about the outpatient clinic. As for the centre and the streets and securing the streets I was told by that Borivoje Jakovljevic. He discussed the securing of roads and the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were Ilic and his colleagues securing in the outpatient clinic in Bratunac? Who were the wounded and sick?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The people in question were of Muslim ethnic background. I told you that he mentioned that a woman literally delivered her child in the outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when it is stated that they were securing the passage of vehicles through Bratunac where the refugees from the enclave of Srebrenica were being sent, is it correct to say that due to antagonisms and poor relations there was an objective danger of letting the refugees from Srebrenica go through the territory controlled by Serb forces unescorted?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you. Without any escort, it would have been dangerous. Certain individual could get strange ideas and cause incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You hail from the village of Opravdici. If I understand correctly it is a part of Kravica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Opravdici village belongs to the local commune of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in that village too on the 7th of January, 1993, horrible things happened against Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know because I, too, participated in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the sentiments that prevailed at the time between the two ethnicities, Serb and Muslim, was there objectively a great degree of danger of people taking revenge and that it was impossible to contain or control the accumulated hatred?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There was hatred, definitely. I can provide an answer to that. However, I do not support taking revenge, and I do not second that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the document before you, it is also stated that night duty, as stated here, was both at the school and in the Fontana hotel. It says the UNHCR school. Let me ask you this: Did you have any knowledge of members of the military police working at that time at a location where UNPROFOR members were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I've no knowledge of they're being accommodated in Bratunac whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night between the 12th and the 13th, in terms of the Fontana hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there between the 12th and the 13th. Between the 11th and the 12th, I was in the environs of the hotel. But the next day, I attended to a different task, which was away from the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it in a different way. Where were you between the 12th and the 13th, during the night?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Providing security for the Fontana hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. Where were you when you say securing the Fontana hotel between the 12th and the 13th? Where was it? Where in the town itself? Or where in the hotel were you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The security operation entailed a wider perimeter. There is immediate security, wider security, road security, et cetera. On the 11th, I was on the first floor of the hotel. On the 12th, for most of the night, between the 12th and the 13th, I was in front or at the back of the hotel but I wasn't at -- in -- on the first floor. I was at the reception of the hotel as well because I tried to catch very brief naps of about half an hour in between shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 13th, in the morning, again, you were tasked with going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you been given that task before by Nikolic, or did someone talk to you on the 13th again saying you have to go back to Potocari? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can explain in detail as to the 12th in the morning. It was conveyed by Mirko Jankovic and supposedly Momir Nikolic was waiting for us in Potocari. I can recall some orders from Momir on the 13th, but as for the morning of the 13th, I know that we were told to go back. We were literally said, Those of you who were in Potocari go back. And that was in front of the military police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told that by your officer, Mirko Jankovic or by Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I am confused between Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic, who was one of the commanders, or maybe Slobodan Mijatovic. But I would have to speculate. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you had the same task on the 13th in Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July at any point in time, and at any location in Potocari, could you observe or see any kind of mistreatment, abuse of the fleeing population?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, do you recall whether food and water was supplied as well by the civilian and military authorities from Bratunac to the fleeing population?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall whether on that day you saw any civilian representatives from Bratunac in Potocari: Ljubisav Simic, Miroslav Deronjic, or Srbislav Davidovic aka Puce?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any of them. As for the first two I know about them, but I don't know this last person, Puce. I don't know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, if, on the 13th of the July, at any point in time you saw Momir Nikolic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, who was physically separating the able-bodied men from the rest of the refugee population?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The procedure was the same, just as it was the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would still ask you to tell us for the record who engaged in it the second day.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The members of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, did you see any VRS members or members of the Bratunac Brigade, or even if we go more widely, taking part in the separation of able-bodied men on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I didn't notice their presence, save for the members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask to look at D24, which is footage. It has already been used with a member of the monitoring mission of the UN. I think it lasted around three minutes, after which I will have a few questions for the witness. We will not rely on the sound, and we have already indicated as such. We're only interested in the video recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll conclude with this part. Your Honours, with your leave, it seems that General Mladic has some stomach problems. Can he be allowed to leave for a very short period, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we -- is it his wish we take an early break? In which case, we will do that. Or does he just want to be absent for two or three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we may, we can take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, first of all, Mr. Mladic can be escorted out of the courtroom. He's the first person interested to leave the courtroom. He can be escorted out. And once security has escorted Mr. Mladic out of the courtroom, the witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll take a break, and -- could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, can we proceed? Yes, of course after the witness has been escorted in. I'm asking because of the reason why we had an earlier break. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, before the break, we showed you an excerpt from a video-clip depicting the distribution of food, i.e., bread to the population of Potocari on the 12th of July. Did this jog your memory, and did this repeat on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to explain. I already mentioned the distribution of food. I remember that on one occasion the van that we had just seen left at the moment when the buses had not arrived yet and food was distributed from that van. I knew some of the people from that logistics platoon. However, all that food that was distributed on the 12th, on the 13th, was happening some 200 metres from the place where this clip was recorded and it was not distributed in this way. I did not receive food, and from the place where I was, I could see that each bread was cut into four pieces and each of the pieces of bread was accompanied by a tin of cold meat, just one little tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you noticed anybody taking food from the population, that they had just received?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how long did you stay in Potocari on the 13th? Until when?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Until late in the afternoon. I left before the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then, on the 13th of July, did you -- spoke to Colonel Jankovic? Did you have any communication with him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, you didn't see or you do not remember having seen General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I can't be sure of the dates anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you left Potocari, was the process of the evacuation of the population finished?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the moment when Colonel Jankovic gave you your new order?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When giving you that order, did Colonel Jankovic tell you to forcibly bring the population should you encounter any people on the road leading from Potocari to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I already told you a couple of hours ago, we were supposed to inform them to come back to the same place in Potocari because there would be a new round of transportation organised for them the following day. That was our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet any of those groups of people or individuals, and did you force any of them to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you had forced them, would that have been contrary to the way you understood Colonel Jankovic's order?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Of course. It would be just the opposite. Our order was to inform people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your assessment, how many people did you come across that evening, on the 13th of July, on the road leading to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You say the road. Yes, it was on the road, but it was only about 2 or 3 kilometres further we saw a few people moving slowly or sitting by the road. We conveyed the message to them. They looked forlorn. They looked concerned. That would be my estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number of people that he came across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the number of the people he came across. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said several dozens, in little groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] it was a request from the interpreters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question that concerns both dates, the 12th and the 13th. While you were in Potocari on those two days, did you hear artillery fire which may have been opened from the general area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the evening when your mission was accomplished, you again found yourself at the command of the military police platoon; is that correct? Did you receive yet another order after that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It would be more correct to say that once we accomplished the mission, when I returned, I found Mr. Momir Nikolic at that same place in the Potocari sector. He had already issued his order that people should not go home but, rather, that we should report to the command of the military police platoon because there were other tasks awaiting us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is very important to know the time. To the best of your recollection, when was that? What time of day on the 13th of July when you spoke to Momir Nikolic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Judging from my previous answer, you can conclude that that was late in the afternoon. First, I accomplished my orders from Colonel Jankovic, and then I talked to Momir Nikolic. It was late in the afternoon. It was still not dark but it was rather late that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had seen Momir Nikolic on the 13th in Potocari before he gave you that order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us - and again, please, let's focus on the precise time - to the best of your recollection, when was it on the 13th of July when you had Momir Nikolic facing you in Potocari, when you saw him in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was on the 13th in the evening, towards the end of the day. And before that, I saw him on several occasions on the 12th and on the 13th, so I can't give you any other times because I had several meeting with him in the course of the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That new order that concerned the night between the 13th and the 14th, who did you get that order from? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We received that order on our return, and when we found ourselves in front of the police command. Momir Nikolic was there. He had preceded us in a car. He told us to join the colleagues at the Vuk Karadzic elementary school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a car. Would I be right in thinking that that was a requisitioned Toyota?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a Mazda or some other Japanese-made car. It was a light blue colour. I don't know where he got it from. After I was given my orders from General Jankovic, my colleagues who were next to Nikolic and next to that car, I heard that he had driven that car out from the UNPROFOR base. I don't know on whose approval. I really wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your recollection, what order was given to you that concerned the night between the 13th and the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The order was to go in front of the Vuk Karadzic school in order to provide security for the persons who were in and around that school. I'm saying in and around the school because, later on, I saw that there were people in the house -- in the school but there were also people around the school, on the streets, in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, when you use the expression "to provide security for the persons who were in and around that school," do you mean to provide security that nothing would happen to them? Or to guard them and to keep them where they were that moment so that they would not move? In which way did you use that expression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said "Stojanovic" and then "Janjic." Was that a correction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I started -- let me see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether I used any name. But could you please answer that question. If you said "providing security," is that to keep them so that they couldn't go from where they were, or is it to protect them from any evil that may have come from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding of the order was to protect them from any evil. To thwart any threat from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answered my question. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up a document from Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez's collection. The number is P01132. The e-court page I'm interested in is 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a photo of the centre of Bratunac. While we're waiting for it to appear, I would like to ask you, sir, to the best of your recollection, where were the refugees accommodated at that moment, or, rather, during that night? What locations did they occupy?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the school, and I heard from my colleagues that the school was full. I didn't see it myself. I heard that from others. I saw them, as you walk from the command towards the centre of town, towards the Fontana hotel. There's a road to the left leading to the police station and passing by the station and leading up to the school. It is about 100 to 150 metres long. There were buses on that street. I know that because I saw them. I went home because I resided very close by across the street from the municipality building. I also saw buses in front of the municipality building, and there were people on the buses. I would like to add to that that there were two, if not three, buses in another location. Across the SUP there was a bakery, and across there, there's a little alley. There used to be a market there, and if you went along that street, you would arrive at the football stadium. In that little alleyway next to the bakery shop there were at least two other buses. I'm sure of that because I could see that from the place where I was stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the photo in -- on the screen in front of you. With all due respect to what you told us previously, would you be able to find your bearings and tell us what facility is encircled in red? Could that be the school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't understand anything in this photo. I could be of assistance by saying that I used to be provided with much clearer photo at the BiH Court. And it was much easier to get my bearings on that map. Maybe you have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my time is really limited. I suppose that we have that photo. I'm not sure that it is. In any case, to the best of your recollection can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the total number of those vehicles in all the locations you have just described for us, those vehicles, the buses where you saw detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I saw about a dozen buses. There was also a lorry. I'm sure that there was one very close to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was your best estimate, would you say that the number of buses was ten and that there was one lorry?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say a dozen, plus a lorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think the witness estimated 12. Not to suggest 10 and 11 -- 10 and one lorry, I'm not quite sure I understand why we are doing that. He gave his estimate: 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I heard in the interpretation was some ten or so, plus a lorry. I apologise if my conclusion was wrong, though it was not my objection to change anything in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought in my interpretation I heard 12. Then if that is the case, I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the words translated was "a dozen." A dozen is from what I understand 12. That's at least my understanding o the word. Let's proceed. It seems not to be a vital issue but Judge Moloto is asking for great provision, and rightly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I just wanted to clarify this for that very reason and now I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I need to ask you one more thing. You remember an incident involving those detainees. Do you remember some sort of shooting? If you do, could you please explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what happened.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: During the night, around midnight, I would say, from the place where I was, I heard from the direction of the school, which was some 70 or 80 metres away from where I was, I heard some men shouting on several occasions. I'll try and tell you what happened and I could hear the word, The people from Glogova, where are you? Glogova is place that I'm familiar with. It sounded like an invitation to a rebellion. Somebody was crying, People from Glogova, are you there? Come out. In any case, the words were more or less the same every time. It happened on several occasions. And then I heard a burst of fire from the same direction from which I heard that voice shouting to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any murders, any killings of the people, either in the buses or in the school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did not see any, and I can state for a fact that nobody was killed in any of those three or four buses and the lorry. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see people being taken off the buses, that they were then ill-treated or abused or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we continue. I'm looking at the clock at this moment and wonder, Mr. Weber, how much time would you need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Probably at the very least five minutes, but up it up to ten depending on answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May be a few questions from the Chamber as well. I don't know how much time you would still need, Mr. Stojanovic, but to ask the witness what he has not seen, if he has not positively stated that he had seen something, then the Chamber will not accept that he had seen other things but assume that he had not seen anything not mentioned. But, of course, that is not, under all circumstances, a reason not to ask someone whether he had seen something. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will abide by the times given, and I will keep the Prosecution in mind. I'll try to wrap things up soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, on the 14th, the convoy with the people who were at the school and on the buses left Bratunac. Did you see the convoy -- the column?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, in your view, in your assessment, how many vehicles were used to transport the people who spent the night between the 13th and the 14th in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think I said that a few times. I wasn't there until the end of their departure. After the first five or six buses left, I left the location too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will try to get an answer from you in this regard: As for the Rocevic school, did you go there on the 14th or the 15th, bearing in mind what you recall as to the moment of convoy departure from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 65 ter document 04205, page 23 of the B/C/S and 20 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We go back to the duty log-book kept by the Bratunac Brigade MP platoon. The date is the 21st of July. If you look at the middle part of the page, it is stated that that day, the military police provided security for the route travelled by General Mladic: "A patrol consisting of eight policemen was engaged in securing the UNPROFOR check-point at the battery factory." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you recall the 21st of July and where General Mladic was going to? In other words, what was the route you secured in terms of his passage?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I think I mentioned today already that when I discussed food and UNPROFOR soldiers while we were doing that, there is a possibility I was there, but I don't have any knowledge or recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's pause for the interpreters. It is our position that we can see on the footage that on the 21st of July UNPROFOR left the Potocari base and went to the Bratunac-Ljubovija bridge and then further afield. And General Mladic was taped as seeing them off. Does this refresh your recollection of any of your work-mates providing security along that stretch of the road to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I really can't recall, and I'd rather not speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The second note says what you've already tried to answer when asked by Judge Orie; in other words, that you, too, at some point in time provided security of the UNPROFOR check-point at the battery factory. That note, does it correspond with your recollection that you, too, were engaged in these tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think I was clear and that I established a link when I said that between the 15th and the 20th I was engaged for several days, perhaps one or two weeks, in Potocari at the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Following these events, did you ever have another occasion to see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will conclude with the following question: Given your impression of what you could hear and see in the course of those few days in Bratunac, what was General Mladic like at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood your question properly. Perhaps you can clarify, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the people in Birac and the villages around Bratunac and Srebrenica? And what was your position or your view of General Mladic? In your words.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It would take quite a lot of time to explain it all, but all I can say is that I am full of praise for his conduct. I have all the best to say about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I seek to tender three pages, if so possible, from the document which is 65 ter 04205. The pages being ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the book of the military police platoon. If you want to -- you have to upload only those pages which are relevant. I see there are 20 pages uploaded in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the entire material is relevant and really should be admitted in full. It relates to the activities of the Bratunac MPs at around the time of the charged offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean in full, let me just say the [Overlapping speakers] ... pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The 20 pages corresponding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, to the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 20 pages translated. Nevertheless, they will have then the B/C/S version is to be uploaded and limited to that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We can take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll take care of that. I take it then that we'll have a new upload. And then already the 20 pages which were translated will receive what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D285 is provisionally assigned number to the still -- to upload 20 pages in both languages. Anything else, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'd like to thank you and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Fluegge has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to clarify one matter. At the end of page 68 of today's transcript, you told us about Mr. Momir Nikolic and that he issued his order about new assignments for you and other members of the military police. What kind of assignment was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The assignment was, and I imagine you're talking about the 13th, after I have completed my task issued by Colonel Jankovic. Nikolic's task was not to stray but to be in front of the military police building, to receive new instructions. As I said already, he did so in front of the MP building. He told us to go in the direction of the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the new assignment you received from him. Did I understand that correctly? Or was there a different, additional assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well, Witness. I'm trying to understand your evidence, what the activities of the military police platoon were during those days. And I have a few brief questions for you. The first one: Was the military police platoon engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, as far as the Vuk Karadzic school, the one I mentioned, that was on the 13th in the evening. That is what I learned from my work-mates, members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the following days? 14th, 15th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my second question would be: Was the military police platoon involved or engaged or busy with the surrender of Muslim people in one of these days?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Kindly explain to me the -- the word "surrender."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "surrender," I understand that people give themselves to another force and put themselves at the disposition of that force.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I will answer to the best of my understanding. As for any surrender, the answer is no. If you mean the take-over of the Srebrenica enclave, we were only engaged in securing the road between Sase and Pribicevac. We were not participating in the take-over the territory. The next day on the 12th we were engaged in securing the location at Potocari as the population was leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is not that people surrendered to your force and then that you accepted them and that you would give them to other elements in the armed forces. That didn't happen. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then was your platoon involved in any way in apprehending Muslims that were hiding in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I heard, although I wasn't present, that there was a search of terrain between Srebrenica and Zepa after all those events concerning the 13th and the 14th. It was at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when -- were then Muslims who were hiding apprehended? I mean the following: If you search the terrain, you may find nothing. You can also search the terrain and then find persons hiding and that you apprehend them. Did the latter happen?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know there was a search of terrain, I'm positive of that. I did not participate in it, and I'm not aware of what the result of it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now in the -- I'm talking about the days following the take-over of Srebrenica, well, up to, I would say, up till the 16th, 17th, 18th of July. Now, was your unit involved in apprehension and perhaps then also securing of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I've said already that I have no such information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you whether the following might refresh your recollection. In the document which received provisionally number D285, I read for the 14th and 15th of July very short description of the tasks: "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." If I go to the 12th and the 13th, I read that: "The police were engaged in securing UNHCR and the surrender of the Muslim people from Srebrenica in Zuti Most to the Serb soldiers in Bratunac." Could I then move on to the 15th. There, I read that -- again, a very short description of what the unit did. It's not much. But what there is in the description is: "The police worked on searching and combing the area, as well as apprehending the Muslims found hiding in the area." Then finally for the 17th of July, I read in what seems to be the log for your unit and which is not very precise in every respect. I read: "One police patrol remained in Bileca to secure and guard the Muslims." And that follows on a line which says: "Patrols worked on apprehension and securing of Muslims in municipal area of Bratunac and Srebrenica." This gives a bit of a different picture compared to your answers. Would you agree with that, and do you have any explanation for the difference between your testimony in this respect and what we find in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This is what I can say. Perhaps the Prosecutor's Office have a clearer picture because they have my statement from the Blagojevic case. Let's say the 12th and the 13th, I have explained my activities in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. I asked you a few questions, four questions. In the questions, I used almost literally the language I find in the log-book. What I find in the log-book and what I heard in your answers, to some extent you said, I wouldn't know; in other cases, you said, No, this is what did not happen. I'm asking your explanation for the difference between what I find in the log-book and the answers you have given me a minute ago, if you have one.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'll happily explain, but I can't be as quick and precise as you. I did not at any time deny what you have read out. It was not my intention to deny certain events or activities. I'm trying to explain, though, why I may not be aware of some of them, if they indeed took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say your answers to the extent you said you didn't know, it's just your lack of awareness. And, apart from that, you do not deny that anything I have read may have happened. Is that ... even if you said that it did not happen in the previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As regards my information, I don't know of certain things. I certainly cannot deny that something may have happened, but the case may have been that I was not informed or was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that. Mr. Weber, we are -- if could you make it five minutes, that would be preferable. Again, we need the indulgence of the -- of those who are assisting us. So could you try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honours. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, today at transcript page 45, you were asked about the special police in Potocari. I'd like to take you to one of your previous answers from the Blagojevic case. On page 9780, you were asked whether they ever informed you or told you who had given the order to carry out activities that you were able to observe them carrying out. That is, the separation of the men from their families. You subsequently stated: "I asked the policemen who were next to me why this was being done. They just explained what I had heard before, that Mladic said that that is the way it -- it would be done" -- sorry. Excuse me, "... that it would be. And that they were working in accordance with the plans." When was it that these special policemen told you that Mladic said that that is the way it would be done?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You're right, I was told that on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And where were you when these special police told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was already in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You make a reference in your earlier testimony that, "... they just explain what I had heard before." What did you hear before, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I heard that from my police members, military police members, who actually told me the same after General Mladic addressed the crowd of people. He said that that the women and children would be transported first and that the men would follow in the course of the day, but later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please quickly have 65 ter 24511.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, being called up onto your screen is an expropriation of materiel supplies order dated 26 September 1995 from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. In the heading of this order, it says that the commander of the Main Staff is issuing this order regarding to the -- related to material supplies from UNPROFOR base in Potocari village. The remainder of this order lists the items that were to be expropriated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. My first question to you is: Are you sure that materials were taken from the UNPROFOR base on the dates that you've described or whether they happened at some time later?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: And what date is that? I said that I was there from the 15th to the 20th and much later and that there were lorries upon lorries leaving the area loaded with the stuff. I really did not pin-point the date, did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. It's not important. In this order, there's no reference to any food supplies being taken. In fairness - and the Prosecution is aware - we do have another document which is not currently on our 65 ter list, which does indicate -- it's date 14 July 1995 from the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade which indicates that there were receptacles for transporting bread, of which there were five, and receptacles for transporting food, for which there were five. Does this information refresh any of your memory with respect to either the date or the items that were present at the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As far as food is concerned, I adhere to my previous statement. There was a huge quantity of food and all that food was unpacked by us. We used this. We served ourselves to it at that time and much later for a long time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time and I'll let the witness stand. However, I would ask just so it's available to the Chamber that we bar table at this time 65 ter 24511, and Ms. Stewart has informed me that the second document, if we could just have it marked for identification for the time being, is 65 ter 28896. And we're happy to wait for further discussions with the Defence concerning whether or not 28896, whether there's any objection or any other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the document on our screen at this moment tendered from the bar table, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not to this document. I'm a little bit confused, Your Honours. This document, 2886 is something that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. This document is now tendered by the Prosecution from the bar table. Madam Registrar, the number would be ... Please remain seated, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24511 receives number P1449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1449 is admitted into evidence. And the other document, where Mr. Weber asked it to be marked for identification, Madam Registrar, was number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P1450, Your Honours. But may I just mention the document is not available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have to wait until a later moment, Mr. Weber. We can't afford at this moment to continue any further. Check whether the document you had in mind is in e-court, and we'll then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time are a changing quickly sometimes. It's now in e-court. Madam Registrar, could repeat the 65 ter number and the provisionally assigned number for this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28896 receives number P1450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, anything else? Any further questions? But even then, I would invite you to keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions arising from the Prosecutor's question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Janjic, this, then, concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You're excused, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had two procedural issues, but I do not dare to raise them at this moment. I thank very much all those assisting us around this courtroom for their patience. And we adjourn. And we resume Tuesday, the 14th of May, in this same courtroom, III, and we'll start at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon and we'll continue until 7.00. We stand adjourned.
